items.title: RFC 3164: The BSD Syslog Protocol
items.creator: C. Lonvick / IETF
items.why: Section 4.1.2 defines the syslog timestamp as 'Mmm dd hh:mm:ss' local time with no year, and section 5.1 concedes that 'neither of these ... addresses the issue of associating a correct timezone with each record' — exactly the gap a parser fills by guessing when it turns 04:10 into 09:40. A 'what is syslog' explainer shows the message shape; this shows why the offset is unknowable from the message itself.
items.struggle: The syslog line has no year and no time zone — how does the SIEM decide what time it was?

items.title: What time zone are the description timestamps in Windows Event log (UTC?)
items.creator: Server Fault
items.why: The asker is doing what your learners will do — comparing the Date column in Event Viewer with a timestamp pasted inside the event message — and the answer separates the UTC event record, the local-time display and the string the service wrote. That third distinction is what settles whether the 04:10 log or the 09:40 alert is the one that is wrong.
items.struggle: Are the timestamps written inside a Windows event description UTC or local time?

items.title: Basic Searching in Splunk Enterprise
items.creator: Splunk How-To (Splunk)
items.why: Under nine minutes of the official walkthrough: run a basic search, move the time range picker, and pull fields into the results — the three controls behind most empty or unreadable result grids. It beats a multi-hour SPL course because it stops at 'did my search even look at the right data', which is the question an empty queue cannot answer for you.
items.struggle: I searched and got 'No results found' even though I know the events arrived.

items.title: Write your first query with Kusto Query Language
items.creator: Microsoft Learn
items.why: Eleven short units teach take, project, where, count and sort against sample tables, so a learner who only knows Splunk's 'stats count by' can see the same counting question as a KQL pipe without a Sentinel tenant. That port is the point of l6-2; a Splunk-only tutorial leaves half the lesson unlearned.
items.struggle: I can write SPL, but my first Sentinel KQL query returns an empty table and I don't know which part is wrong.

items.title: Elasticsearch term query does not give any results
items.creator: Stack Overflow
items.why: A self-described Elasticsearch beginner's term filter on 'title' returns nothing while the same filter on another field works, and the answers explain analyzed text versus exact keyword terms. This is why a field=value habit carried over from Splunk silently matches zero documents in Elastic instead of raising an error.
items.struggle: My Elasticsearch term query returns no results even though I can see the matching document.

items.title: SOC Alert Triage Explained: What Most Beginners Get Wrong
items.creator: MyDFIR
items.why: Four minutes on triage itself rather than on a vendor console, pitched at the mistakes a first-time analyst makes on the way to a disposition. It is short enough to watch before a shift, and it makes the point the l6-3 ticket turns on: a verdict needs evidence, not a rule name.
items.struggle: How do I decide in three minutes whether an alert is a true positive or a false positive?

items.title: Finding the “Goldilocks” Zone: A Practical Approach to Alert Triage
items.creator: Hayden Covington / Black Hills Information Security
items.why: An associate director of security operations writes about the two ways a shift actually fails — spending too long on one 'too hot' alert and too little on a 'too cold' one — and gives a severity-led order for allocating limited time. It beats generic 'triage steps' posts because it is about the queue, not the single alert.
items.struggle: I have 40 alerts in the queue and no idea which one deserves the next 20 minutes.

items.title: SOC Alert Tuning and False Positive Reduction: Setting Yourself Up for Success
items.creator: SANS Cyber Defense
items.why: SANS authors Justin Henderson and John Hubbard break false-positive reduction into a methodical programme — prepare, choose the right tooling, then tune — rather than a bag of tricks, across a recorded live stream. That is the l6-4 shift: a noisy rule is tuning input, not a closure reason.
items.struggle: The same rule fires 40 times a week and everyone just closes it — how do I fix the rule instead of the ticket?

items.title: Rules | Sigma Detection Format
items.creator: SigmaHQ
items.why: Shows a detection as a small YAML document with logsource, selection, condition, falsepositives and level — the concrete form of 'an alert is a sentence and a detection is a test of it'. The falsepositives field is the artifact beginner rules omit and then drown in.
items.struggle: How do I write a rule that finds the behaviour rather than today's IP address?

items.title: Brute Force, Technique T1110 - Enterprise | MITRE ATT&CK
items.creator: MITRE ATT&CK
items.why: The page a beginner should land on instead of the matrix poster: T1110 with its four sub-techniques (guessing, cracking, spraying, stuffing) shows how one behaviour splits into the log lines actually seen. Naming T1110.003 for a spray across many accounts is a different escalation from calling 412 failures 'a brute force alert'.
items.struggle: Which ATT&CK technique is 412 failed logons for one service account, and does the sub-technique matter?

items.title: The Pyramid of Pain
items.creator: David J. Bianco (Enterprise Detection & Response)
items.why: The canonical ranking of why a blocked IP or hash costs an attacker minutes while forcing a TTP change costs days — the shelf-life argument behind judging an indicator by its age. It beats 'IOC vs TTP' listicles because it gives a hierarchy to reason with, not two definitions.
items.struggle: We blocked the IP from the alert — why did the attacker come back the next day from a new one?

items.title: Blue Team Handbook: SOC, SIEM, and Threat Hunting (V1.02): A Condensed Guide for the Security Operations Team and Threat Hunter
items.creator: Don Murdoch (GSE #99)
items.why: A condensed field guide written for the analyst on shift rather than the architect: SOC workflow, SIEM use and the questions to ask before trusting an alert. It is the only item here that follows a case from queue to escalation to handover, which is why it takes the one paid slot.
items.struggle: What does a competent SOC handover actually contain at the end of a shift?
